newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - EU probes German post office freight pricing.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU probes German post office freight pricing.

text.p: The German post office has come under investigation for predatory pricing allegedly aimed at eliminating competing package delivery companies, according to documents obtained by Reuters on Monday.

The investigation was sparked by a 1994 complaint from United Parcel Service, the freight and parcel carrier of the United States, which accused Deutsche Post AG of unfair pricing in an attempt to squeeze out competitors.

In a letter to Deutsche Post (DPAG), the European Commission's competition department said it intended to take a "negative position" on a complaint that the German postal service illegally offsets parcel rates with high rates for letter mail.

"On the basis of preliminary assessment, we believe that DPAG has engaged in unlawful predatory pricing," the Commission wrote. It added that the use of cross-subsidised rates since at least 1984 "indicated an intention by DPAG to eliminate its competitors."
Reuters obtained a copy of the letter and Deutsche Post AG confirmed its contents. A Deutsche Post spokesman pointed out that Brussels had not reached any final decision.
"This is only one step toward a decision," the spokesman told Reuters. "The EU has not reached a final ruling yet."
He also said the German cartel office had already investigated Deutsche Post and found no illegal subsidies.
But the EU Commission said Deutsche Post covered losses in freight delivery, where it faces competitors, with high rates for letters. DPAG holds a legal monopoly on letter delivery.
"These cross-subsidies are clear, persistent, deliberate, finanaced by a monopoly position and have a substantial exclusionary effect," the Commission wrote.
Paul Friedhoff, a member of the Free Democrats (FDP) in parliament, said Deutsche Post covers more than two million marks in parcels losses per year with "excessive" letter rates.
The FDP, junior member of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government, wanted to end Deutsche Post's monopoly on letter delivery, Friedhoff said.
"The preservation of this monopoly allows 98 percent of postal delivery to go on without competition, and keeps open only two percent of the market," he said.
Deutsche Post chief Klaus Zumwinkel said on Monday in the German news weekly Focus that ending the letter monopoly would force many post offices to close.
United Parcel Service filed the complaint to the Commission in 1994, alleging Deutsche Post charged parcel rates that are less than its actual costs.
A finding in its favour could affect other legal monopolies with units in competitive industries, UPS vice president of public affairs Anton van der Lande said.
The Commission said it would send a formal statement of objections from Deutsche Post in April, and could reach a decision by next autumn.

Deutsche Post claimed it could not be held accountable for the period before 1994, because the German government fixed postal rates before then. But Brussels said it reserved the right to review price policies both before and after that date.
